'''Nicholas John Phillips''' (26 September 1933 – 23 May 2009) was an English [[physicist]], notable for the development of photochemical processing techniques for the colour [[hologram]]. Holograms typically used to have low [[signal-to-noise ratio]]s, and Phillips is credited as the pioneer of [[silver halide]] holographic processing techniques for producing high-quality reflection holograms.

==Career==
Phillips graduated with a [[Bachelor of Science|BSc]] degree in physics from [[Imperial College]], London.{{cn|date=October 2026}} He was a senior researcher at the [[Atomic Weapons Research Establishment]] (AWRE), [[Aldermaston]], from 1959 to 1962. He was a research scientist at the [[Sperry Corporation#Sperry Rand|Sperry Rand Research Centre]], [[Sudbury, Massachusetts]], United States, from 1962 to 1963. He was a theoretical physicist at [[English Electric]], [[Whetstone, Leicestershire|Whetstone]], [[Leicester]], UK, from 1963 to 1965.{{cn|date=October 2026}}

From 1965 to 1993, he was appointed at [[Loughborough University]], where he rose to Professor of Applied Optics.{{cn|date=October 2026}} In October 1993, he was appointed as Professor of Imaging Science at [[De Montfort University]], [[Leicester]], UK. Phillips was the co-founder in the early 1970s of Holoco, who using lasers supplied by [[The Who]] (that had been used in laser light shows during their concerts), constructed the ''Light Fantastic'' exhibitions as [[Royal Academy|The Royal Academy of Arts]], London, in 1977–8.{{cn|date=October 2026}}

The company became Advanced Holographics in 1980 when The Who withdrew their financial backing, and was based in [[Loughborough]], UK,<ref>M. Kodera, "Holography in Japan," ''Leonardo'', '''Vol. 25''', No. 5, Archives of Holography: A Partial View of a Three-Dimensional World: Special Issue. (1992), pp. 451–455.</ref> and later became part of Markem Systems.<ref name="Johnston">{{cite book |last=Johnston |first=Sean |title=Holographic Visions: A History of New Science |year=2006 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=0-19-857122-4 |pages=360 }}</ref>

==Research and achievements==
Phillips is credited with the development of bleaching and processing techniques, which made it possible to
record multi-color reflection holograms from a single wavelength [[laser]].<ref>D. Jung, "Holographic space: A historical view and some personal experiences, ''Leonardo'', '''Vol. 22''', No. 3/4, Holography as an Art Medium: Special Double Issue. (1989), pp. 331–336.</ref> His research interests include holographic displays, edge-lit holograms, optical encoding for security, photopolymers, and novel micro-optic systems, and he has numerous patents in these areas.<ref>D. Abbott, B. R. Davis, N. J. Phillips, and K. Eshraghian, "Simple derivation of the thermal noise formula using window-limited Fourier transforms," ''IEEE Trans. Education'', '''39'''(1) (1996) pp. 1–13.</ref>

==Holographic art==
Phillips developed a technique for producing white light holograms that work in dim lighting conditions, which are now widely used in  the world of holographic art.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20080226015947/http://www.holonet.khm.de/benyonarchive/reviews/recoyl3.htm From Apparition, Holographic Art in Australia<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

==Awards==
Phillips was awarded the [[Institute of Physics]] [[Young Medal and Prize|Thomas Young Medal]] (1981) in recognition for contributions to holography, particularly the development of high quality holograms for visual display.  He is a Fellow of the [[Institute of Physics]].

==Selected publications by Phillips==
* N. J. Phillips and D. Porter, "An advance in the processing of holograms," ''Journal of Physics E: Scientific Instruments'' (1976) p.&nbsp;631
* N. J. Phillips, A. A. Ward, R. Cullen, and D. Porter, "Advances in holographic bleaches," ''Photographic Science and Engineering'', '''24''' (1980) p.&nbsp;120.
* N. J. Phillips, H. Heyworth, and T. Hare, "On Lippmann's photography," ''Journal of Photographic Science'', '''32''' (1984) pp.&nbsp;158–169.
* N. J. Phillips and R. A. J. van der Werf, "The creation of efficient reflective Lippmann layers in ultra-fine grain silver halide materials using non-laser sources," ''Journal of Photographic Science,'' '''33''' (1985) pp.&nbsp;22–28,
* N. J. Phillips, "Benign bleaching for healthy holography," ''Holosphere,'' '''14'''(4) (1986) p.&nbsp;21.
* N. J. Phillips, "The silver halides—the workhorse of the holography business," ''Proceedings of the International Symposium of Display Holography,'' '''3''' (1988) p.&nbsp;35.
* [[Derek Abbott|D. Abbott]], [[Bruce R. Davis|B. R. Davis]], N. J. Phillips, and [[Kamran Eshraghian|K. Eshraghian]], "Simple derivation of the thermal noise formula using window-limited Fourier transforms," ''IEEE Trans. Education,'' '''39'''(1) (1996) pp.&nbsp;1–13.
